newsitem.title: USA: Georgia Senate okays revenue debt for universities.
newsitem.headline: Georgia Senate okays revenue debt for universities.

text.p: The Georgia Senate has approved a bill allowing the Georgia Education Authority to issue up to $250 million of revenue bonds for capital projects, Sen. Mark Taylor said Wednesday.

The measure passed 42-7 in the Senate on Tuesday and now heads to the House. It would amend a 1949 law that created the education authority, making it more of a true financing agency than a policy setting body.

Like several other Georgia agencies, the education authority is already authorized to issue revenue bonds. But "as a matter of policy and practice," Georgia has relied almost exclusively on general obligation debt for the last two decades, said Tim Burgess, of the state office of planning and budget.

Because the state constitution caps GO bond debt at 10 percent of revenues collected during the previous budget year, or about $250 million, universities have had to compete with other state entities for GO bond authorizations, even for projects such as parking garages and dorms that were to be repaid entirely from designated revenue streams. That often caused delays in badly needed projects, supporters of the bill said.
"This will set up a separate category in our budget where we will set aside projects that will be financed through revenue bonds. It applies only to the universities," said Taylor, D-Albany.

Taylor, who is Gov. Zell Miller's Senate floor leader, objected to a newspaper characterization of the bill as a circumvention of the state's GO debt cap. He said it would set a separate $250 million cap on revenue debt issued by the education authority.

The new law would also require that revenue bond-financed projects be approved by the Board of Regents, the governor and the General Assembly, in order "to satisfy concerns about the unfettered use of revenue bonds," Burgess said.
